question:
An 68-year-old male presents with episodes of anxiety and palpitations lasting 30 to 60 minutes,
resolving spontaneously. These episodes have occurred intermittently over several months, often
triggered by stressful situations. His medical history includes hypertension managed with amlodipine,
hyperlipidemia treated with simvastatin, and anxiety for which he takes venlafaxine. During an episode,
physical examination reveals a regular heart rate of 110 beats per minute, blood pressure of 153/84
mm Hg, temperature of 36.2°C, and oxygen saturation of 97% on room air. The patient appears
anxious and mildly diaphoretic, but the rest of the examination is unremarkable. Laboratory results
show a plasma metanephrine level of 0.32 nmol/liter (reference range: <0.5) and a plasma
normetanephrine level of 2.0 nmol/liter (reference range: <0.9). What is the most likely cause of this

patient’s laboratory findings? Answer Choices: (A) Pheochromocytoma (B) Age-related sympathetic
overactivity (C) Paraganglioma (D) Essential hypertension (E) Autonomic dysfunction (F)
Hyperthyroidism (G) A medication effect (H) Adrenal incidentaloma (I) Carcinoid syndrome (J) Anxiety
 A. Anxiety
B. Autonomic dysfunction
C. Paraganglioma
D. Pheochromocytoma
E. Hyperthyroidism
F. Essential hypertension
G. A medication effect
H. Adrenal incidentaloma
I. Carcinoid syndrome
J. Age-related sympathetic overactivity
